motion: Must God's possibility be demonstrated before belief in God can be rationally justified?

bridges.burden: Show that God cannot be rationally accepted as an explanation before God's possibility is demonstrated.
bridges.successCriterion: Establish a truth-directed justification rule that excludes unverified supernatural candidates without merely assuming atheism.

bridges.burden: Explain what makes a method reliable enough to justify belief.
bridges.successCriterion: Connect justification to testability, falsifiability, independent confirmation, replication, or comparable truth-tracking controls.

bridges.burden: Explain why explanatory fit alone does not make an entity a live candidate explanation.
bridges.successCriterion: Show that unconstrained or unverified causes can fit observations without supplying rational warrant.

bridges.burden: Separate faith as confidence from faith as an evidential method.
bridges.successCriterion: Preserve the agreed rationality of some confidence while showing why confidence itself supplies no warrant.

bridges.burden: Distinguish understandable belief on limited information from objectively warranted confidence.
bridges.successCriterion: Tie rational justification to available evidence and likely truth rather than sincerity or internal consistency alone.

bridges.burden: Show that standard comparative inference can justify theism without a separate prior demonstration of God's possibility.
bridges.successCriterion: Defend an ordinary abductive or Bayesian route from evidence to theism and explain why the proposed possibility screen is not an additional rule of rational inquiry.

bridges.burden: State a positive account of rationally acceptable belief.
bridges.successCriterion: Ground belief in direct evidence or support from other rationally acceptable beliefs.

bridges.burden: Explain how evidence can compare theism with alternatives.
bridges.successCriterion: Show that priors and likelihoods can be exposed, updated, and applied to theism as to other hypotheses.

bridges.burden: Clarify that the defended faith is trust or confidence rather than belief without evidence.
bridges.successCriterion: Preserve common ground that evidence-based confidence can be rational and avoid defending faith as a freestanding method.

bridges.burden: Test the consistency of the possibility requirement against historical and scientific inference.
bridges.successCriterion: Identify ordinary cases where a candidate is assessed through evidence without a separate prior possibility proof.

sections.title: Faith, rationality, and shared ground
sections.weightRationale: The opening definitions fix what is and is not disputed and prevent the nominal question about all faith from replacing the narrower motion.

sections.title: Truth-directed standards of justification
sections.weightRationale: The speakers develop the evidential and reliability standards that make the later possibility dispute intelligible.

sections.title: Possibility and ordinary inference
sections.weightRationale: Examples involving wheels, history, diamonds, and aliens directly test what a demonstration of possibility requires.

sections.title: The Higgs analogy and supernatural candidates
sections.weightRationale: The central clash asks whether scientific inference supplies a model for theism or instead presupposes independently grounded candidate kinds.

sections.title: Bayesian comparison and candidate testing
sections.weightRationale: The exchange isolates whether explanatory likelihood can overcome a very low or unestablished prior and whether investigation must precede candidate status.

sections.title: Updating, convergence, and fine-tuning
sections.weightRationale: The final independent exchange applies the rival methods to evidential convergence and fine-tuning before the excluded moderator branch begins.

moves.speaker: Blake Giunta
moves.claim: The Christian faith under discussion ordinarily means trust rather than belief without evidence.
moves.warrant: Giunta appeals to ordinary Christian usage, biblical reference works, the Greek term, and biblical exemplars who are portrayed as having evidence while remaining figures of faith.
moves.inference: If faith is evidence-compatible trust, its rationality cannot be rejected merely by defining it as blind belief.
quoteEligibleExactSpans: the word faith in sort of folk terms it means trust
they all saw incredible miracles and things that constituted really good evidence
moves.attributionRationale: This is a continuous portion of Giunta's opening statement, before Dillahunty's opening begins.
moves.importanceRationale: It fixes an important subsidiary definition and preserves the shared acceptance of rational confidence, but does not by itself resolve the possibility requirement.

burdenContact.rationale: It directly defines the kind of faith Giunta is defending as evidence-compatible trust.

moves.speaker: Blake Giunta
moves.claim: A belief is rationally acceptable when it is directly evident or well supported by other rationally acceptable beliefs.
moves.warrant: Perceptual seemings, memory, intuition, and elementary knowledge can provide direct starting points from which further beliefs are supported.
moves.inference: Rationality can be built recursively from evident starting points without requiring every proposition to be independently demonstrated first.
quoteEligibleExactSpans: B is directly evident to s at T
new beliefs can be built from beliefs that you've acquired that way
moves.attributionRationale: Although the moderator briefly asks for clarification, the selected passage is Giunta's uninterrupted opening explanation and contains no substantive opponent turn.
moves.importanceRationale: This is Giunta's positive epistemic standard and supplies a central alternative to a separate possibility demonstration.

burdenContact.rationale: It states the foundational and inferential routes by which beliefs become rationally acceptable.

moves.speaker: Blake Giunta
moves.claim: The relevant inquiry is which side has the better reasons, not whether either side can demonstrate its conclusion in advance.
moves.warrant: Giunta frames the question as whether there is a possible circumstance in which religious trust is rational and proposes following where the evidence points most strongly.
moves.inference: Comparative support can rationally move confidence even without a prior conclusive demonstration.
quoteEligibleExactSpans: there are better reasons to think that faith can be rational
we just want to have an idea who has the best case
moves.attributionRationale: This is the closing portion of Giunta's opening statement.
moves.importanceRationale: It previews the con side's motion-level rejection of an extra prior-demonstration screen.

burdenContact.rationale: It expressly substitutes comparative evidential support for a requirement that possibility be separately demonstrated.

moves.speaker: Matt Dillahunty
moves.claim: Confidence can be rational, but calling confidence faith risks switching from a confidence level to faith as its own justification.
moves.warrant: Dillahunty distinguishes confidence based on presentable reasons from treating faith itself as the epistemic foundation and warns that ordinary religious usage moves between those senses.
moves.inference: Agreement that some confidence is reasonable does not establish faith as a reliable route to warranted belief.
quoteEligibleExactSpans: if all you mean by faith is confidence
the reason I believe is because of faith
moves.attributionRationale: This is a continuous portion of Dillahunty's opening response.
moves.importanceRationale: It narrows the dispute and blocks a definitional shortcut while conceding the shared point about confidence.

burdenContact.rationale: It separates faith as a confidence label from faith offered as the reason for belief.

responseComponents.rationale: Dillahunty accepts rational trust in principle but argues that the term's shifting use does not vindicate it as a source of warrant.

moves.speaker: Matt Dillahunty
moves.claim: A case for rationality requires a demonstration even though a rational process can still lead to a false conclusion.
moves.warrant: People, including audiences of a magician, can draw reasonable conclusions from the evidence available to them while being misled.
moves.inference: Subjective reasonableness is not enough; justification needs an evidential demonstration tied to the claim.
quoteEligibleExactSpans: make a case for something being reasonable or rational without a demonstration
you can reach a write a conclusion rationally and it still be the wrong conclusion
moves.attributionRationale: This passage remains within Dillahunty's opening statement.
moves.importanceRationale: It states the pro side's motion-level demand for demonstration and distinguishes it from mere psychological confidence.

burdenContact.rationale: It makes demonstration foundational to the kind of rational justification relevant to the motion.

responseComponents.rationale: It rejects the suggestion that comparative reasons can replace demonstration by arguing that rational appearance can be mistaken.

moves.speaker: Matt Dillahunty
moves.claim: Faith used as a foundation cannot discriminate reliably among beliefs.
moves.warrant: The same appeal can support incompatible denominations or morally abhorrent claims, whereas people with good reasons can present those reasons directly.
moves.inference: A bare faith appeal is not a truth-tracking justification and should not inherit the rationality of evidence-based confidence.
quoteEligibleExactSpans: if faith were the foundation then you would find yourself saying
I could take any position and root it by just saying
moves.attributionRationale: This is a continuous argument in Dillahunty's opening statement and explicitly notes that Giunta is not defending the target usage.
moves.importanceRationale: It supports the definitional boundary and reliability standard without assigning Giunta a position he disavows.

burdenContact.rationale: It explains why faith as a freestanding basis cannot be treated like evidence-based trust.

moves.speaker: Blake Giunta
moves.claim: Both speakers agree that a person can rationally hold religious confidence given that person's experiences.
moves.warrant: Giunta uses Paul's reported transformative experience as an example of evidence that could rationally support Paul even if the event's truth is not thereby settled for others.
moves.inference: The question must concern the adequacy of a person's evidence, not a blanket claim that religious confidence is inherently irrational.
quoteEligibleExactSpans: we agree on probably the most important point
given his experience could well have been rational
moves.attributionRationale: Giunta explicitly takes the floor after the moderator opens dialogue, and Dillahunty's answer begins after the selected endpoint.
moves.importanceRationale: It records a necessary concession that prevents either side from being scored on the broader nominal question.

burdenContact.rationale: It anchors the defended view in experience-based confidence rather than unsupported belief.

responseComponents.rationale: Giunta accepts Dillahunty's distinction and identifies agreement that evidence-based confidence can be rational.

moves.speaker: Matt Dillahunty
moves.claim: A person can reason understandably from limited information yet still lack a truly justified confidence level.
moves.warrant: Lucky-sock and psychic examples show that incomplete evidence can make a false conclusion seem reasonable to the believer.
moves.inference: The relevant standard must distinguish a reasonable-looking process from evidence that objectively supports the conclusion.
quoteEligibleExactSpans: based on the limited information they have
your process but incomplete to the point where you can reach a wrong conclusion
moves.attributionRationale: Dillahunty begins with an explicit qualification and speaks continuously until Giunta's response.
moves.importanceRationale: It refines the shared ground into a truth-directed standard that later motivates independent checks.

burdenContact.rationale: It distinguishes subjective rationality under limited information from warranted confidence.

responseComponents.rationale: It grants possible subjective reasonableness but denies that this alone establishes objectively supported confidence.

moves.speaker: Matt Dillahunty
moves.claim: Rational justification should require a plausible conviction that is likely true and comports with reality, not merely internal consistency.
moves.warrant: A minimal standard based on what a person can manage licenses conclusions from insufficient information, whereas a higher reasonable-person standard better approaches truth.
moves.inference: Justification should be calibrated to objective evidential support rather than personal capability alone.
quoteEligibleExactSpans: justifiable plausible conviction that this is true or likely true
merely being internally consistent is not really that much of value
moves.attributionRationale: After a brief self-directed aside, this is Dillahunty's uninterrupted account of rationality.
moves.importanceRationale: It defines the truth-directed justification standard that bears directly on whether a possibility screen is warranted.

burdenContact.rationale: It grounds justification in likely truth and reality rather than coherence or sincerity.

moves.speaker: Blake Giunta
moves.claim: The productive question is what circumstances would make belief that God is trustworthy justified.
moves.warrant: Both speakers already agree that people can rationally reach false beliefs given their data, so the remaining task is to identify sufficient conditions for justification.
moves.inference: The debate should move from general psychological rationality to a shared analysis of justified theistic belief.
quoteEligibleExactSpans: when can we reach a justified belief in something like God
ideal circumstances good circumstances sufficient circumstances
moves.attributionRationale: Giunta summarizes the preceding agreement and poses the next question; Dillahunty begins answering after the endpoint.
moves.importanceRationale: It narrows the discussion to the actual burden and invites the criterion that becomes the motion-level dispute.

burdenContact.rationale: It asks for the sufficient evidential conditions under which theistic belief is justified.

responseComponents.rationale: Giunta accepts that reasonable processing can produce false belief and redirects to conditions of justification.
He asks for concrete sufficient conditions for the truth-directed standard Dillahunty has described.

moves.speaker: Matt Dillahunty
moves.claim: A justified claim needs sufficient evidence appropriate to its nature, including testability, falsifiability, and independent verification where possible.
moves.warrant: Extraordinary source claims such as Paul's experience cannot be distinguished from delusion without checks, while mundane claims need less evidence because their kind is already familiar.
moves.inference: Reliable justification varies with the claim but requires methods capable of discriminating the proposed source from alternatives.
quoteEligibleExactSpans: a claim is testable if and only if it's also falsifiable
one factor is definitely independent verification as much as possible
moves.attributionRationale: The passage is Dillahunty's extended answer, including a brief dog aside but no substantive opponent argument.
moves.importanceRationale: It supplies the central reliability criteria behind the pro route and the later exclusion of supernatural candidates.

burdenContact.rationale: It identifies concrete truth-tracking controls for rational acceptance.

responseComponents.rationale: It answers Giunta's request by specifying evidence, falsifiability, claim sensitivity, and independent verification.

moves.speaker: Blake Giunta
moves.claim: Dillahunty's apparent standard says that belief in an explanation is justified only if the explanation is demonstrated possible and delivered by a reliable method.
moves.warrant: Giunta synthesizes Dillahunty's stated concern with reliable evidence into two proposed necessary conditions and asks what demonstrating possibility amounts to.
moves.inference: The possibility condition can now be tested separately from the shared requirement of reliable inquiry.
quoteEligibleExactSpans: X is demonstrated to be possible and the belief is a deliverance of a reliable method
what does it take for X to be demonstrated to be possible
moves.attributionRationale: Giunta explicitly introduces a synthesis of Dillahunty's position and retains the floor through the question.
moves.importanceRationale: This crystallizes the exact motion-level rule the rest of the debate examines.

burdenContact.rationale: It isolates the contested prior-possibility condition from the uncontroversial reliable-method condition.

responseComponents.rationale: Giunta converts Dillahunty's reliability answer into an explicit two-part necessary-condition rule for examination.

moves.speaker: Matt Dillahunty
moves.claim: Possibility need not be established by direct observation of the exact case; reliable categorical similarity and inference can establish it.
moves.warrant: Even with a covered casino wheel, knowledge of comparable wheels and incentives supports conclusions about what outcomes are plausibly available.
moves.inference: The prior-possibility requirement permits ordinary inference from known kinds and is not a demand to observe the target entity in advance.
quoteEligibleExactSpans: I'm fine with categorical similarities
information inferences are fine and categorical inferences are fine
moves.attributionRationale: This is Dillahunty's answer to Giunta's request for clarification, with no substantive speaker change.
moves.importanceRationale: It clarifies the pro motion burden and blocks the charge that possibility must be proven by circularly producing the very object at issue.

burdenContact.rationale: It explains how the required possibility demonstration can be inferential and category-based.

responseComponents.rationale: It answers what a possibility demonstration can consist in by allowing reliable categorical inference.

moves.speaker: Blake Giunta
moves.claim: Historical belief tests whether Dillahunty's demonstration requirement can accommodate justified inference about unrepeatable facts.
moves.warrant: Historical events cannot generally be reproduced, yet people regard many historical propositions as rationally justified from reports.
moves.inference: If the rule cannot explain ordinary historical warrant, it may be too restrictive or insufficiently specified.
quoteEligibleExactSpans: is it rationally justifiable to believe in a historical fact
do they meet the definition of demonstrated
moves.attributionRationale: Giunta asks a bounded challenge before Dillahunty begins answering.
moves.importanceRationale: It is a subsidiary consistency test of the possibility rule using a familiar nonexperimental domain.

burdenContact.rationale: It tests the proposed rule against accepted historical inference.

responseComponents.rationale: It asks whether inferential demonstration by known kinds extends coherently to historical reports.

moves.speaker: Matt Dillahunty
moves.claim: Historical claims are justified provisionally through reports, source reliability, inference, and independent or adverse-source corroboration.
moves.warrant: A report that Alexander gave a speech is stronger when independent sources with opposed interests agree than when it comes from one biased side.
moves.inference: The demonstration standard can accommodate historical reasoning because it asks for discriminating evidence rather than experimental repetition alone.
quoteEligibleExactSpans: rely on inferences and the reports that we have
if it's a biased source
moves.attributionRationale: Dillahunty gives a continuous response to the historical example.
moves.importanceRationale: It answers a subsidiary analogy and reinforces the general reliable-evidence route.

burdenContact.rationale: It identifies source comparison and corroboration as truth-tracking controls in history.

responseComponents.rationale: It explains how demonstration in history consists of qualified reports, inference, and corroboration.

moves.speaker: Matt Dillahunty
moves.claim: A composite scenario is a live possibility when its important components are independently known possible; unknown components block that conclusion.
moves.warrant: Diamonds, burial, and backyards are known kinds, while an Alpha Centauri alien and its travel introduce unverified variables.
moves.inference: Theism cannot receive an initial possibility status merely because its description is not yet disproved; its central variables need independent support.
quoteEligibleExactSpans: every aspect of that is independently possible
you would need to show that the primary variables are independently possible
moves.attributionRationale: The examples and explanation are continuously delivered by Dillahunty.
moves.importanceRationale: This is the clearest positive account of what the pro side means by establishing possibility.

burdenContact.rationale: It specifies the independent-component test that underwrites the required possibility demonstration.

moves.speaker: Blake Giunta
moves.claim: Dillahunty's criterion entails that theists cannot justifiably reach supernatural belief unless possibility is first demonstrated in his required way.
moves.warrant: Giunta explicitly applies the independent-possibility condition to supernatural belief and notes that theists have not met the specified prior task.
moves.inference: The proposed rule is a decisive filter, so Dillahunty must justify imposing it rather than treating it as a neutral clarification.
quoteEligibleExactSpans: requires first the demonstration of possibility
theists can't or a person can't justifiably reach belief in the supernatural
moves.attributionRationale: Giunta summarizes the consequence and hands the position back to Dillahunty at the endpoint.
moves.importanceRationale: It exposes the exact practical consequence of the motion-level rule and places its justification at issue.

burdenContact.rationale: It identifies the rule as an additional exclusionary condition on theistic justification.

responseComponents.rationale: It shows that the independent-component test excludes supernatural belief before comparative evidence is assessed.

moves.speaker: Matt Dillahunty
moves.claim: The supernatural has not been demonstrated real or possible and is less grounded as a candidate than a natural alien hypothesis.
moves.warrant: Aliens at least fall within natural categories and known physical constraints, whereas a God proposal may invoke something outside those established categories.
moves.inference: God cannot be treated as a justified best explanation until a basis for its candidate possibility is supplied.
quoteEligibleExactSpans: I know of no way to demonstrate that the supernatural is real or is even possible
aliens from Alpha Centauri are necessarily more plausible than a God
moves.attributionRationale: Dillahunty confirms Giunta's reconstruction and develops the alien comparison until Giunta asks to state his own view.
moves.importanceRationale: It directly applies the pro motion rule to God and explains the claimed asymmetry between natural and supernatural candidates.

burdenContact.rationale: It asserts that the prerequisite for justified theistic explanation remains unmet.

responseComponents.rationale: Dillahunty accepts that the rule currently excludes supernatural belief and offers the natural-category contrast as justification.

moves.speaker: Blake Giunta
moves.claim: Standard deductive, inductive, abductive, and Bayesian methods permit inference to God without a separate rule requiring possibility to be demonstrated first.
moves.warrant: Giunta says these academically developed methods already govern evidence-based belief and he cannot locate Dillahunty's extra requirement within them.
moves.inference: Unless independently defended, the prior-possibility filter should not override ordinary comparative reasoning about theism.
quoteEligibleExactSpans: there's no rule that corresponds to what you've in the past identified as being a rule
it's nowhere to be found out here
moves.attributionRationale: Giunta explicitly puts his cards on the table and speaks until Dillahunty's science response.
moves.importanceRationale: This is the con side's principal motion-level objection to treating possibility as a separate prerequisite.

burdenContact.rationale: It denies that the possibility screen is part of otherwise accepted rational methods.

responseComponents.rationale: It asks why an independently unsupported filter should prevent standard inference from evidence to theism.

moves.speaker: Matt Dillahunty
moves.claim: The Higgs was a legitimate scientific candidate because its constituent variables were physical, its hypothesis was testable, and acceptance followed evidential demonstration.
moves.warrant: The proposal did not appeal outside known physical categories and collider evidence could confirm it or support an alternative explanation.
moves.inference: Scientific hypothesis generation does not refute the possibility requirement; it illustrates provisional candidacy followed by evidence-based acceptance within established kinds.
quoteEligibleExactSpans: the Constituent variables of that were known physical
it is not rationally justified to accept it as the explanation
moves.attributionRationale: Dillahunty introduces science and develops the Higgs answer continuously.
moves.importanceRationale: It supplies the pro side's central scientific analogy and distinction between candidacy and justified acceptance.

burdenContact.rationale: It argues that a candidate's known physical basis and testability distinguish it from an unconstrained supernatural proposal.

responseComponents.rationale: It claims scientific practice already respects the relevant constraint through known constituent kinds and deferred acceptance.

moves.speaker: Blake Giunta
moves.claim: Dillahunty uses the possibility requirement as a catch-all objection to theistic evidence in a way that would be circular if applied to the Higgs.
moves.warrant: Giunta says he offers data more expected on theism, yet Dillahunty refuses the conclusion until God's possibility is separately shown; an analogous demand would require the Higgs field before evidence for it.
moves.inference: Evidence bearing comparatively on a hypothesis should itself be allowed to support that hypothesis rather than being screened out by a prior duplicate demand.
quoteEligibleExactSpans: there's this catch-all philosophical objection
you'd have to demonstrate there's a Higgs field first before he can give evidence for it
moves.attributionRationale: Giunta lays out the analogy and asks Dillahunty to locate the disconnect.
moves.importanceRationale: It is a direct, developed challenge to the coherence of the pro side's motion-level prerequisite.

burdenContact.rationale: It tests the possibility rule against the evidential path by which scientific entities are inferred.

responseComponents.rationale: It argues that requiring the entity before its supporting evidence would mishandle the very scientific analogy Dillahunty invokes.

moves.speaker: Blake Giunta
moves.claim: CERN evidence supports the Higgs through comparative likelihood, the same evidential form Giunta uses for theism.
moves.warrant: The collider data are more likely if a Higgs field exists than if it does not, just as Giunta claims his data are more likely on theism than on atheism.
moves.inference: The form of inference does not itself justify excluding theism before its likelihood evidence is considered.
quoteEligibleExactSpans: this data is more likely on the hypothesis that there's this Higgs field
I'm doing the exact same thing when I make the case for God
moves.attributionRationale: Giunta asks about the direct evidence and then states the likelihood analogy; Dillahunty's answer begins at the next event.
moves.importanceRationale: It gives the positive comparative-inference argument supporting the con route, rather than only criticizing the possibility screen.

burdenContact.rationale: It explicitly maps the comparative likelihood structure from the Higgs case to theism.

responseComponents.rationale: It contends that both hypotheses are supported by asking whether observed data are more expected given the hypothesis.

moves.speaker: Matt Dillahunty
moves.claim: The supernatural differs from the Higgs because no confirmed supernatural kind supplies constraints that make it a testable candidate explanation.
moves.warrant: Tests of psychics and dowsers could establish an unexplained ability, but would not identify a supernatural source; investigation could proceed through natural hypotheses, while there is nothing confirmed to point to as supernatural.
moves.inference: Matching an observation to a supernatural story does not supply the independent basis required for justified candidate status.
quoteEligibleExactSpans: we can't begin to hypothesize about supernatural explanations
we have nothing to point to where we can say here's what the supernatural is
moves.attributionRationale: Dillahunty directly answers the claimed symmetry and develops the dowsing example continuously.
moves.importanceRationale: It states the pro side's strongest claimed asymmetry between scientific and supernatural hypotheses.

burdenContact.rationale: It argues that without a confirmed kind, supernatural labels do not constrain or identify an explanation.

responseComponents.rationale: It denies inferential symmetry because the Higgs belongs to a constrained physical framework while the supernatural lacks an independently confirmed referent.

moves.speaker: Matt Dillahunty
moves.claim: When known candidate causes fail, ignorance of a cause does not make God a plausible explanation.
moves.warrant: Matches and blowtorches are grounded causes of a burning table; if investigation finds none, 'we do not know' remains preferable to a cause that has not itself been shown possible.
moves.inference: Explanatory sufficiency or the absence of rivals cannot substitute for independent warrant that the proposed cause is a live candidate.
quoteEligibleExactSpans: the answer is we don't know
it doesn't mean that there's any good reason to think that that is even a possible explanation
moves.attributionRationale: Dillahunty develops the burning-table example after Giunta asks for elaboration.
moves.importanceRationale: It makes the candidate-constraint rationale concrete and directly challenges inference from unexplained data to God.

burdenContact.rationale: It distinguishes grounded candidate causes from an unconstrained gap-filling proposal.

moves.speaker: Blake Giunta
moves.claim: Standard Bayesian and abductive reasoning can compare both the Higgs and theism without a special rule barring the latter from candidacy.
moves.warrant: For each hypothesis, one asks how likely the data are if it exists versus if it does not; a vague category such as 'magic' should be replaced with a specific causal proposition.
moves.inference: Once the hypothesis is stated precisely, ordinary likelihood comparison is the appropriate test of its explanatory support.
quoteEligibleExactSpans: I think the right approach is as you know a standard Bayesian approach
there's no rules that would prevent theism from being a candidate
moves.attributionRationale: Giunta responds directly and speaks through his request for a specific proposition.
moves.importanceRationale: It is the main positive methodological defense of treating theism as a candidate before a separate possibility demonstration.

burdenContact.rationale: It applies the same likelihood questions to scientific and theistic hypotheses.

responseComponents.rationale: It argues that a precise causal hypothesis, unlike the label 'magic,' can be assigned priors and likelihoods and compared with alternatives.

moves.speaker: Matt Dillahunty
moves.claim: A hypothesis designed to entail the data can have a high likelihood without being a warranted candidate cause.
moves.warrant: A fire-casting wizard makes a burning table expected, but the relevant question is whether the person can start fires mentally; investigation must establish that capacity before the story becomes a functional explanation.
moves.inference: Likelihood fit conditional on a hypothesis cannot replace evidence for the hypothesis's causal capacity or prior possibility.
quoteEligibleExactSpans: how likely is it that that person can actually cause things to start fires
until I can show that this person can start fires with their mind
moves.attributionRationale: Dillahunty supplies the specific wizard proposition Giunta requests and carries the example through its conclusion.
moves.importanceRationale: It directly answers the Bayesian proposal by separating data likelihood from warrant for the candidate itself.

burdenContact.rationale: It argues that a hypothesis's explanatory fit must be preceded by evidence that the proposed causal capacity is real.

responseComponents.rationale: It concedes that a tailored hypothesis predicts the data but denies that this establishes its candidacy or causal warrant.

moves.speaker: Matt Dillahunty
moves.claim: Bayesian analysis is useful in constrained domains but cannot justify supernatural or cosmic-origin conclusions when priors and comparable cases are unavailable.
moves.warrant: There is only one observed universe, and a hypothesis can make the observed result certain without thereby being the right explanation, as a cheating-card story can make thirteen spades expected despite a fair deal remaining possible.
moves.inference: A high conditional probability under theism does not by itself yield a justified posterior explanation of the universe.
quoteEligibleExactSpans: I don't think it it should go anywhere near the territory of the supernatural or cosmic origins
we have one universe so we got no priors
moves.attributionRationale: After Giunta asks whether this is a critique of Bayesian analysis, Dillahunty gives a continuous domain-limitation answer.
moves.importanceRationale: It provides a separate critique of applying Bayesian machinery where priors and reference classes are disputed.

burdenContact.rationale: It argues that the method lacks the empirical constraints needed to be reliable in the target domain.

responseComponents.rationale: It accepts Bayesian usefulness generally while denying that the cosmic-supernatural application has grounded priors or comparisons.

moves.speaker: Blake Giunta
moves.claim: Bayesian analysis already penalizes ad hoc hypotheses by assigning them low priors.
moves.warrant: A wizard hypothesis may predict the fire, but its improbability is transferred into the prior probability of the hypothesis itself.
moves.inference: The candidate need not be excluded before analysis because the framework contains an internal mechanism for discounting poorly grounded explanations.
quoteEligibleExactSpans: sufficiently ad hoc that has a sufficiently low prior probability
you've transferred all of the improbability over on to the hypothesis itself
moves.attributionRationale: Giunta takes up Dillahunty's wizard example and states the Bayesian treatment of ad hocness; Dillahunty's next objection begins afterward.
moves.importanceRationale: It directly answers the concern that explanatory flexibility automatically gives an exotic hypothesis undue support.

burdenContact.rationale: It explains how priors constrain flexible hypotheses inside the proposed method.

responseComponents.rationale: It says the wizard's tailored fit is not free because the same implausibility appears in its prior.
It maintains that priors, rather than a separate categorical ban, are the proper place to register background implausibility.

moves.speaker: Blake Giunta
moves.claim: Bayesian reasoners may begin with different subjective priors but should converge as shared evidence accumulates, and theism can be assessed in the same way.
moves.warrant: Scientific experts can disagree from different priors despite shared information; explicit priors plus continued updating make those assumptions visible and allow convergence.
moves.inference: One may start with any prior for theism and still reach rational confidence if enough favorable evidence accumulates, without a separate possibility criterion.
quoteEligibleExactSpans: they have different priors and what Bayesian analysis does of course is forces them to expose those priors
if enough evidence accumulates you get to the conclusion that theism is probably true
moves.attributionRationale: Giunta answers the frequentist objection and develops the updating argument continuously.
moves.importanceRationale: It supplies the mature con account of how initially disputed plausibility is handled through transparent updating.
